Hashub
HASH-ub
proper noun
Hebrew Chashshub (H2815), considerate or thoughtful — from chashab (H2803), to think, to devise, to reckon, to impute; the verb behind it was counted unto him for righteousness.

Biblical Definition

Hashub is the name of several men in the records of the restoration, most of them builders. One repaired a section of Jerusalem's wall with Malchijah the son of Harim, including the tower of the furnaces (Neh 3:11); another, named with Benjamin, repaired over against their house (Neh 3:23); a Hashub sealed the covenant of Nehemiah 10 (Neh 10:23); and Hasshub of the sons of Merari is named in the Levitical genealogy as an ancestor of Shemaiah, a Levite dwelling at Jerusalem (Neh 11:15; 1Ch 9:14). The detail in Nehemiah 3:23 is the one worth dwelling on: they repaired the wall over against their house. Nehemiah's method was to set each family to the stretch of wall nearest its own door, so that a man's labour and a man's stake stood in the same place. The name means considerate, from chashab, to think and to reckon — a good name for a builder, since a wall is what happens when somebody has thought it through. Scripture uses the same verb for God's reckoning: Abraham believed, and he counted it to him for righteousness (Gen 15:6).

Origin & Era

The name of several men of the restoration, builders on the wall of Jerusalem and sealers of the covenant. It means considerate or thoughtful.

expand to see more

HASHUB, Hebrew Chashshub, considerate, thoughtful; also written Hasshub.

1. A builder who repaired a piece of the wall and the tower of the furnaces.

2. One who with Benjamin repaired the wall over against their own house.

3. One of those who sealed the covenant in the days of Nehemiah.

4. Hasshub of the sons of Merari, in the Levitical genealogy at Jerusalem.

Key Scripture

Neh 3:11 — "Malchijah the son of Harim, and Hashub the son of Pahathmoab, repaired the other piece, and the tower of the furnaces."

Neh 3:23 — "After him repaired Benjamin and Hashub over against their house. After him repaired Azariah the son of Maaseiah the son of Ananiah by his house."

Neh 11:15 — "Also of the Levites: Shemaiah the son of Hashub, the son of Azrikam, the son of Hashabiah, the son of Bunni;"

1Ch 9:14 — "And of the Levites; Shemaiah the son of Hasshub, the son of Azrikam, the son of Hashabiah, of the sons of Merari;"

Modern Corruption

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Nehemiah's: a man builds best on the stretch of wall nearest his own door.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Hashub is contested by nobody. What his verse contests is a modern habit of moral attention: the tendency to care intensely about distant causes while the nearest duties go undone. It has never been easier to be exercised about a wall a thousand miles away and to leave one's own gate off its hinges.

Nehemiah's arrangement was deliberate. Families repaired the wall in front of their own houses, which meant that the quality of the work and the safety of the family were the same question, and no man could do a careless job at somebody else's expense. Scripture orders duty the same way throughout: if any provide not for his own, and specially for those of his own house, he hath denied the faith, and is worse than an infidel (1Ti 5:8), and as we have therefore opportunity, let us do good unto all men, specially unto them who are of the household of faith (Gal 6:10). The principle to recover is that nearness creates obligation, and that the section of wall over against your own house is the one God has given you to build.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Chashshub (H2815), from chashab (H2803), to think, devise, reckon, impute.

expand to see more

Hebrew chashab (H2803) — to think, to reckon, to impute; he counted it to him for righteousness (Gen 15:6).

Hebrew Chashshub (H2815) — considerate; builders and covenanters of the restoration, Nehemiah 3:11, 3:23, 10:23, 11:15.

Hebrew chomah (H2346) — a wall; the work of Nehemiah 3, divided house by house.

Hebrew Merari (H4847) — the Levitical house that bore the boards and sockets of the tabernacle.

Greek logizomai (G3049) — to reckon, to impute; the New Testament counterpart of chashab in Romans 4.

Usage

"“Hashub the son of Pahathmoab, repaired the other piece, and the tower of the furnaces”."

"“After him repaired Benjamin and Hashub over against their house”."

"“Shemaiah the son of Hashub, the son of Azrikam” — a Levite of the sons of Merari."
